comments.author: warmstart
comments.text:
For those who haven't read it yet: the trick is that each spreadsheet row is one machine step, and the whole program is a single array formula that computes row N+1 from row N. Memory is a wide range of columns, registers are named cells. Recalculation is the clock.

It's a Turing tarpit, obviously, but it's a beautifully documented one. The calling convention section alone is worth the click.

replies.author: iferror
replies.text: OP here — "recalculation is the clock" is a better one-line summary than anything I wrote. Stealing it for the README. The worst part was pointers: dereferencing means an indirect lookup per access, and the formula engine's dependency tracker assumes you'd never do such a thing. Load-bearing INDIRECT everywhere.

replies.author: warmstart
replies.text: How do you handle stack overflow? Genuinely asking — do you just run out of columns?

comments.author: rowmajor
comments.text: I did something adjacent for a compilers course: a tiny Forth in formulas, at forthcell.example.com. The dependency-graph recalculation model is secretly a dataflow machine, which is why this works better than it has any right to. The formula engine is doing topological scheduling for free.

comments.author: bitrotting
comments.text: Skeptic take: fun hack, but the article claims this is "useful for environments where you can only ship a spreadsheet." If your deployment target is a spreadsheet, the fix is organizational, not a C compiler.

replies.author: cellwise
replies.text: You'd think so, but I've worked places where the spreadsheet WAS the approved runtime and getting a real program deployed took two quarters. People build tunnels where the walls are.
